response.query: Which g‑methods best identify mediation when mediators are serial or time‑varying and confounders are affected by exposure?
response.answer: The g-formula and targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) are best g-methods for identifying mediation with serial or time-varying mediators and confounders affected by exposure. They adjust for time-varying confounding effectively.

results.title: A Tutorial on Causal Inference in Longitudinal Data With Time-Varying Confounding Using G-Estimation
results.content: G-estimation of structural nested mean models adjusted for time-varying confounding and loss to follow-up were employed to estimate the average treatment effect of periodontal therapy on subsequent tooth extractions. This broad class of methods pioneered by James Robins has deep roots in causal inference research and is widely used in (bio)statistics, epidemiology, and medical sciences to assess time-varying treatment effects in longitudinal data when treatment-dependent confounding is present (Clare et al., 2018;Wijn et al., 2022). Moreover, we describe how the parametric g-formula may be used to estimate a marginal structural model whose causal parameters parsimoniously encode time-varying treatment effects. Estimating Curvilinear Time-Varying Treatment Effects: Combining G-Estimation of Structural Nested Mean Models With Time-Varying Effect Models for Longitudinal Causal Inference. The proposal combines two established but unconnected approaches for assessing treatment effects in longitudinal designs: g-estimation of structural nested mean models (from the causal inference literature) and time-varying effect models (from the behavioral sciences and psychotherapy literature). G-estimation of structural nested mean models can resolve treatment-dependent confounding but requires correctly specifying whether and how the causal effects change over time. Using data from observational studies to estimate the causal effect of a time‐varying exposure, repeatedly measured over time, on an outcome of interest requires careful adjustment for confounding. This study describes methods to estimate causal direct and indirect effects and reports the results of a large Monte Carlo simulation study on the performance of the ordinary regression and modern causal mediation analysis methods, including a previously untested doubly robust sequential g-estimation method, when there are confounders of the mediator-to-outcome relation. The aim of many longitudinal studies is to estimate the causal effect of a time varying exposure on an outcome that requires adjusting for time varying confounding. Time varying confounding affected by previous exposure often occurs in practice, but it is usually adjusted for by using conventional analytical methods such as time dependent Cox regression, random effects models, or generalised estimating equations, which are known to provide biased effect estimates in this setting. This article explains time varying confounding affected by previous exposure and outlines three causal methods proposed to appropriately adjust for this potential bias: inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting, the parametric G formula, and G estimation.
